review_text_raw:
Okay, while I said I liked this game, [b]I think in terms of recommendation, this is more a "maybe" than an outright "yes."[/b] There are several things to consider before you purchase this one, and while I ultimately think you'll enjoy the experience either way, you may be slightly frustrated by at least one or two of these points. I know I was. 

(-) First, the game is short. It took me less than 4 hours to finish it, and that's with several long cut scenes. Speaking of those cut scenes... pay attention to them. I didn't, because some of them seemed pointless, and that led me to the only time I felt truly stuck in this game LOL.

(+) You play as an operator in the FDI, and the entire gameplay involves sitting in front of your computer, connecting dots, and solving puzzles. I absolutely loved it. It was fresh and interesting, and the feeling of things connecting and unraveling was really fun. I actually wish we had more of it—I would've gladly played more hours of more cases, slowly connecting them to this huge conspiracy. It made me hope that someone would make an entire mystery murder game (as opposed to a conspiracy) as "the guy in the chair," slowly unraveling everything and helping the "heroes" solve the mystery. 

(-/+) For a game that's sitting in front of your computer... the stakes are high and so is the tension. I actually got really anxious at parts, in a way that doesn't really happen with most games because, the way everything is set up, WE are Tenner. So I felt like there was a gun aimed at [i]me[/i] at times, LOL. For me, this was a point in favor of the game, but if you're looking for a more relaxed experience, this may not be it. 

(-/+) The ending. Personally? Not a fan. Oh, I loved the reveal. The minute [i]I[/i] started connecting the dots, my stomach dropped. 10/10 for that. But everything after that?... I will be playing the next game, if there is one, but overall, [spoiler]I am not really the kind of person to enjoy an "everybody died" ending. After all the brilliant puzzle solving, I wanted these characters to have a good ending. I have seen people talk about how this was actually a good ending - how Hal is still thwarting the organization 30 years later, and that's realistic and optimistic but damn. I got attached to [i]these[/i] characters. I wanted to see them happy, even if we fail to totally crush the bad guys in the end of the game. And I wanted to understand what the goal of the "bad guys" in this game is, and I don't. They're evil people, but... why are they doing what they're doing? No clue. Which is another thing I don't like. For me, a game needs to be able to stand on its own, even if it's part of a larger narrative. [/spoiler] Essentially, this felt like a game meant to [i]set up[/i] another game, and truthfully, I don't like that.

review_text_raw:
I have very mixed feelings regarding this game, mostly because the play time is so short at about 3 hours.

The game is a bit of a paradox in that it is incredibly well made, with a level of attention to detail that shows a high degree of passion and care went into making it, while at the same time being incredibly short.   Think of a AAA game with only the first level.  Clearly the quality is top-notch but it's a bit baffling someone would put so much work into something so short.  This makes it almost feel like a long demo.

I really liked most of the game, and there is a level of attention to detail and craftsmanship present that all but the best indy titles usually lack. If there was more story so that the game ran 10-20 hours, it would be an easy 9/10, $40+, best game I've played this year. In it's current state, however, I feel like its worth about $10.

So, given its currently priced at $14, what's my final conclusion?  Tepid recommend.  I loved every minute, but given that there were so few of them, I feel a bit conflicted given the price.

I just really hope to see more in the future from this developer.  Make an Operator 2 with at least 10 hours of runtime, price it at ~$30 and you'll have me banging down your door to play.

Also, for those wondering, the game plays like a linear narrative adventure.  Your choices don't matter, but there is some light puzzling and detective work to keep you engaged. The game seems heavily inspired by Hacknet and Orwell, which is a great thing in my book.

Edit: Oh yes, I should mention it runs flawlessly on Windows 7

Excellent game. As others have said (including the developer) it is a very short game and no replayability (unless like me you wanted to get the achievements you missed) but it's £10 and I enjoyed my time with it enough.

Not every game needs to be 40+ hours long with hundreds of DLCs or live service.  Long games often outstay their welcome long before you finish them. With that said, I think in a way the story is impacted by it being slightly too short (story spoilers ahead): 

[spoiler]You're almost immediately thrust into a conspiracy in your first day of the job. It could have done with a few decoy run-of-the-mill cases to get you into the swing of things and get you used to your, supposed, identity and relationships with other characters. Most characters are introduced as an immediate part of the conspiracy. It didn't need too much more so that it runs the aforementioned risk of becoming stale, but a few more short cases for character development wouldn't have hurt.  

I also think the opening cut scene spoils the twist of your identity in my opinion, as soon as it became clear the medical testing was about implanting and overwriting memories, I remembered the first cut scene and guessed what was coming.[/spoiler]

A suggestion for the few like me who do replay it, there needs to be a way to skip cut scenes and dialogue. It was a real slog to get to the mid/late section of the game where I'd missed the achievements. 

All in all, well worth what I paid for it. A short, tight narrative game that held my interest all the way through and a novel, unique experience.

--- BUY THIS GAME WHEN IT IS ON SALE ---

I paid ~ $13.00 and that is TOO much for this game. I think a fair price for this game is $5.00 due to play hours and lack of replayability.

PROs:

+ I like investigative puzzle games and this one was intriguing.
+ Story was compelling.
+ I liked the idea of using different systems to discover information and link said information together.
+ I am looking forward to a sequel. Hopefully it will be longer than this game.

CONs:

- I beat it twice in 7 hours so average game play time was 3.5 hours. I really only played it twice to get the achievements though.
     - I don't think the price of the game should be this high for such a short game. Especially since there isn't a lot of replayability with this game :/.
- The story gives the illusion of choice but regardless of dialogue options, you still end up where you are intended to go; very RAILROADY
- The game has investigative tools but for most of them you only use them once throughout the entire game.
- For my second playthrough, I was REALLY wanting a skip button for scenes where the protagonist "goes home at the end of the day;" It was really boring to sit through those scenes.
- There are some locked files that you don't get access to, which was disappointing. There were many missed opportunities to build lore or give players opportunities to poke around, even if they resulted in dead ends, it would have been nice to fill out the world a little more.
- It would have been nice if there was a reward/punishment system for being smart or needing to have your hand held through the whole game. Some sort of variable input that would impact the game based on player actions. Like a trust meter so if people trust you, it is easier to lie to them or something.

I know it sounds like I am taking a huge dump on this game but my goal is to help the developers with the sequel.The game has A LOT of good ideas, I just think the execution and the offering could have been better.

That being said, I liked the game and I want to see more from this developer.

review_text_raw:
Conspiratorial thinking is kinda like anime girls. Like, okay. So there's this super hot princess from planet catgirl who's on the run from the space mafia, and she just so happens to teleport naked right into your bathtub. While you're in it. And because of this, she's super into you for some reason. Yeah, sounds nice, but this is so insanely removed from how actual relationships form, it's like watching aliens mate (I mean... she is an alien, so...)

And with conspiracies it's like: okay, so there's this ultra-powerful cabal of politicians, billionaires and celebrities, who completely control the society without being spotted... but then they reveal themselves by using symbols in plain sight. And the person to stop them? A bumbling born-into-wealth TV-star who in fact is a 5D-chess player, so all his obvious mistakes are actually genius moves that you just don't get. I don't know guys, seems very legit, but there are a few pieces of this story that make me question its validity.

Think about how a real conspiracy of this scale would work. Incomprehensible wealth would be poured into world-class assassins and operatives to ensure compliance or silence. Evidence would be erased with brutal efficiency, with red herrings and multiple layers of scapegoats; but even then, people are people, and eventually something could possibly slip the cracks. 

The Operator explores this more realistic portrayal of conspiracies, with the scale also being somewhat more realistic. You don't know who you can trust and who you can't. But not everyone (except you) is in on it.

Right?

But hold on. Before you start yelling LOOMINARTY CONFIRMED and smoking dat 420 MLG style, some actual work needs to be done. You're an [strike]FBI[/strike] FDI operator with an access to a pretty sweet database, but also a job to do - to support agents in the field. Whatever confirming of loominarty you'll be doing will have to be squeezed in between protecting and serving those who [strike]are supposed to[/strike] protect and serve. Or perhaps these things could be related?

Wouldn't that be convenient.

Even with all your state-of-the-art tech you'll still have to think outside the box here. And pay attention. You might not find the all-seeing eye, but a funny detail here, a reappearing pattern there, and you just might find something that you're not supposed to.

But it's a dangerous game. For you, and for whoever [i]they[/i] might see as your ally. Things might get tense. Your palms will sweat, your heart will go a little bit faster. Someone's life might be on the line. And you're the only one that picked up the phone.

Still: this little journey might have what you could call flaws. I won't tell you what they are, because I think they don't really alter the value of the experience. You're a clever person; I'm sure you can see what I mean.

(if you're not that clever, you might want to skip this one, I've seen some really funny comments on the forums from people getting stuck because they missed some stuff)

And if my words alone don't convince you, you might want to know that the (achievement-sourced) percentage of people who have beaten the game is 67%. The only game with a number higher than this is Linelith, but that's a puzzle game that can be beaten in an hour. Draw your own conclusions.
